paper_title: Learning from Automatic 3D Gaussian Splatting Edits for Online Bayesian Scene Change Detection

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Online scene change detection requires integrating incoming observations to determine which regions have changed relative to a reference scene. We update change beliefs as new images arrive using generalised Bayesian evidence fusion. However, the prior probability of change and evidence models are unknown beforehand, and numerical Bayesian inference can be costly. We address these challenges by learning offline from automatic edits to a reference 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) model. These edits generate labelled training views without manual annotations. Together with unchanged reference observations, they provide supervision for learning scene-specific evidence models and estimating the effective pixel prior and response statistics. Online prediction combines current evidence with historical support, while closed-form local Bayes factors, parameterized by the learned response statistics, update an accumulated 3D Gaussian field. Object-guided refinement produces the final change masks. Our method achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on PASLCD and CCS3D, with $67.64\%$ and $75.82\%$ mIoU, respectively. On PASLCD, the complete pipeline runs at $17.2$\,FPS over complete query sequences, the fastest among the evaluated online methods. Project page: https://changruizhu96.github.io/work/lego-scd/

sections.title: ABSTRACT
sections.content: Online scene change detection requires integrating incoming observations to determine which regions have changed relative to reference scene. We update change beliefs as new images arrive using generalised Bayesian evidence fusion. However, the prior probability of change and evidence models are unknown beforehand, and numerical Bayesian inference can be costly. We address these challenges by learning ofﬂine from automatic edits to reference 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) model. These edits generate labelled training views without manual annotations. Together with unchanged reference observations, they provide supervision for learning scene-speciﬁc evidence models and estimating the effective pixel prior and response statistics. Online prediction combines current evidence with historical support, while closed-form local Bayes factors, parameterized by the learned response statistics, update an accumulated 3D Gaussian ﬁeld. Objectguided reﬁnement produces the ﬁnal change masks. Our method achieves stateof-the-art accuracy on PASLCD and CCS3D, with 67.64% and 75.82% mIoU, respectively. On PASLCD, the complete pipeline runs at 17.2 FPS over complete query sequences, the fastest among the evaluated online methods.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Scene change detection identiﬁes physical changes in an environment from images captured at different times. When captures follow different camera trajectories, viewpoint and visibility differences complicate direct image comparison (Lu et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026). reference 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) model (Kerbl et al., 2023) enables rendering the earlier scene at query viewpoints, providing common view for comparison. Recent methods, such as MV3DCD (Galappaththige et al., 2025) and O-SCD (Galappaththige et al., 2026b), integrate multi-view change cues by optimizing per-Gaussian change parameters, using batch and online processing, respectively. In O-SCD, processing each new image requires iterative optimization using current and replayed observations, adding computational overhead during online inference. However, updating predictions as new evidence arrives does not inherently require repeated parameter optimization. This motivates updating change beliefs as new images arrive. Generalised Bayesian inference (Bissiri et al., 2016) provides framework to combine prior probability of change with incoming evidence. Putting this idea into practice requires prior and models that translate image differences into change evidence, which are unknown beforehand. We estimate these quantities ofﬂine using automatic reference 3DGS edits and unchanged observations. The edits turn the reference representation into source of labelled training views, supporting scene-speciﬁc learning without manual change annotations. This reduces dependence on large labelled datasets for training single evidence model across diverse scene appearances and changes. The learned evidence models also support efﬁcient Bayesian evidence accumulation. Evaluating Bayesian evidence can require numerical integration or sampling (Kass & Raftery, 1995), adding substantial cost when repeated for incoming frames. We apply the learned evidence models to unchanged reference observations to estimate response statistics, which parameterize local Bayesian model that admits closed-form Bayes factors. We combine current evidence with historical support for prediction and use these Bayes factors to update the ac1 cumulated ﬁeld for subsequent queries. These updates require neither online backpropagation nor past-image replay. Finally, object-guided reﬁnement sharpens boundaries and completes missed object regions. Our method achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on PASLCD and CCS3D, with 67.64% and 75.82% mIoU, respectively. On PASLCD, it outperforms O-SCD Online by 18.40 mIoU points while running at 17.2 FPS, compared with 14.4 FPS for O-SCD Online. Without reﬁnement, the pixel output achieves 60.36% mIoU at 27.9 FPS. Our complete method also exceeds GS-Diffs reported 64.40% mIoU (Galappaththige et al., 2026a) without requiring post-change reconstruction. Given an existing reference reconstruction, automatic editing and model ﬁtting take approximately 3.6 minutes per PASLCD instance on average.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Scene change detection. Image-pair methods identify changes through correspondence and appearance comparison. GeSCF uses SAM features and mask matching without task-speciﬁc training (Kim & Kim, 2025), while SceneDiff compares objects across beforeafter captures using semantic and geometric information (Wu et al., 2026). reference 3D representation additionally enables comparisons at matched viewpoints and integration across observations. 3DGS-CD associates image-level detections across views (Lu et al., 2025), and SCaR-3D combines change cues through multi-view voting and pruning (Zhou et al., 2026). MV3DCD optimizes Gaussian change channels from collection of post-change images (Galappaththige et al., 2025); O-SCD extends this approach to streaming queries, updating change parameters using current and replayed observations (Galappaththige et al., 2026b). CL-Splats uses detected changes to guide local updates of Gaussian scene representation (Ackermann et al., 2025). GS-Diff instead compares geometry and colour between independently reconstructed scene states (Galappaththige et al., 2026a). Our method accumulates evidence on the reference Gaussians without online optimization or past-image replay. Learning from synthetic changes and 3D editing. CYWS constructs training pairs from object segmentation data (Sachdeva & Zisserman, 2023a), while CYWS-3D generates paired observations from synthetic 3D scenes (Sachdeva & Zisserman, 2023b). Both use synthetic supervision to train change detectors that generalize to unseen scenes, requiring training data to cover diverse scene appearances and changes. Advances in 3DGS segmentation (Ye et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2025), editing (Chen et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2025), and relighting (Liang et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2024) enable controlled scene modiﬁcations. RoboSplat edits Gaussian scenes and varies their appearance to train robot policies (Yang et al., 2025), while Zanjani et al. (2025) insert Gaussian objects into driving scenes to train 3D detectors. Given prebuilt reference 3DGS and its associated unchanged observations, we generate labelled changes through automatic edits and ﬁt scene-speciﬁc evidence models and prior ofﬂine. This allows learning to focus on the appearance and response statistics of each reference scene, rather than requiring single evidence model to cover many different environments. Bayesian evidence accumulation. Bayesian updates provide way to combine successive observations with existing beliefs. In scene mapping, POCD updates probabilistic object states using geometric and semantic information to track changes and maintain volumetric maps (Qian et al., 2022). Bissiri et al. (2016) provide generalised Bayesian framework that connects observations to belief updates through loss function. For online time-series changepoint detection, Altamirano et al. (2023) construct generalised Bayesian updates with closed-form posterior parameters using diffusion score matching. We apply generalised Bayesian prediction to scene change detection, using ofﬂine-learned response statistics to evaluate local Bayes factors in closed form for accumulation on reference Gaussians.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION AND LIMITATIONS
sections.content: Our method learns scene-speciﬁc evidence models and statistics from automatic reference 3DGS edits, using the reference scene as source of supervision for online change detection. These learned quantities enable closed-form local Bayes factors and generalised Bayesian history accumulation without online backpropagation or past-image replay. It outperforms O-SCD on PASLCD and CCS3D, achieving 67.64% mIoU at 17.2 FPS on PASLCD. However, our direct object edits and simple relighting prioritize short ofﬂine preparation and may not cover real changes or unusual lighting conditions. Accumulating evidence on the unchanged reference geometry limits how accurately newly introduced objects and occlusion boundaries can be represented in the ﬁeld. The response uncertainty and spatial covariance models are working approximations. Although local Bayes factors are evaluated analytically under the residual model, the fused scores combine dependent evidence and are not guaranteed to be calibrated probabilities of real-world changes. Future work will explore more advanced 3DGS segmentation, editing, and relighting to improve object masks and broaden the generated changes, while assessing whether the resulting detection gains justify the additional ofﬂine preparation time.

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: In this work, generative AI tools were used to assist with initial methodology discussions and exploratory brainstorming, algorithm and code implementation, preliminary manuscript drafting, and textual reﬁnement for grammar, phrasing, and readability. sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: This work uses existing scene-change benchmarks. Incorrect predictions can lead to missed changes or unnecessary follow-up inspections.

sections.title: REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
sections.content: The implementation records reference camera assignments, synthetic events, ﬁtted scene models, effective-prior parameters, and per-image results. All scene-speciﬁc parameters are frozen before target evaluation. The appendices specify the observation transformations, statistical approximations, update order, and effective-prior estimation used for the reported method.

Current-view evidence Ct gives strong responses around candidate changes, including some unchanged regions. Historical support Ht adjusts these responses using earlier observations, while the scene-ﬁtted prior π determines the evidence threshold for predicting change. The fused pixel probability Qpixel reduces false positives but can also suppress true changes, as frame 25 illustrates. Across this 25-frame sequence, mean IoU increases from 47.31% with Ct alone to 57.84% after fusion. Figure 10 complements the quantitative component ablations in Table 3.
